images.text:
Peter: Wow! That was one amazing movie! John, did you enjoy it?
John: I won't lie, it did surpass my expectations. However, there were some crazy scenes, which were confusing.
Peter: Which parts?
John: There were was some talk about nebulas and galaxies, which I still can't quite understand.
Peter: Good question! Galaxies are much larger in size compared to a nebula.
John: Oh okay. That makes sense, but wait ... The main character talked about how he passed by a nebula that was lying inside a galaxy.

Peter: Yes. A nebula can be found inside a galaxy. The same can't be said about galaxies being inside a nebula, which I explained is smaller.
John: This is interesting stuff. I'd love to learn more about galaxies. Peter, I'll make a deal with you. If you'll teach me astronomy, I'll let you off the hook on your proposition.
Peter: Okay deal. I'll have to check my schedule, which looks very busy this month.
John: Well that's too bad. If you won't do it this month, the deal is off.

Peter: Why are you so bent on having it this month?
John: I have to keep my interest high. If you won't find some time for me next month, you can forget about it altogether.
Peter: Fine. I'll give you an hour a week, which is still asking a lot.
John: I don't know if one hour is enough to be honest. If you'll do it for two hours a week, you can expect me to pay for your next movie.
Peter: Sounds very enticing! How about if I come to your house once a week for two hours, will that be okay for you?
John: Fine. Thanks.

You use a non-defining relative clause when you want to add extra information to the noun you are talking about. You need to separate the main clause from the relative clause with commas.

You can create a non-defining relative clause if the relative clause gives more information about a proper noun or a noun that is known. A non-defining relative clause adds non-essential information about the noun.

who or whom (subject or object) = refers to people
which (you cannot use that) = refers to things
whose = shows possession for both people and things

Examples:
The relative clause can come after the subject of the sentence.
Barack Obama, who is the president of the United States, always makes wonderful speeches.
The Bahamas, which is made up of several tiny islands, is a popular tourist destination.

The relative clause can come after the object of the sentence.
Last week I met Barack Obama, who is the president of the United States.
I just came back from the Bahamas, which is made up of several tiny islands.
Notice the difference in meaning between defining and non-defining relative clauses:

A teacher took her students to the beach. The students, who wanted to go swimming, ran into the water.
(This means all of the students ran into the water. This is extra information about the students.)

A teacher took her students to the beach. The students who wanted to go swimming ran into the water. The other students had a picnic in the shade.
(This means that some of the students wanted to go swimming. The relative clause is necessary to define or say which students ran into the water.)
In speaking, remember to pause when you see the commas.
The same can't be said about galaxies being inside a nebula, which I explained is smaller.
I'll have to check my schedule, which looks very busy this month.
Will and Won't in the If-Clause to Express Refusal or Strong Disapproval
If you want to show refusal or disapproval, you can use will and won't in the if-clause of your sentence.

Will can be used to express insistence when you use it with if. Insisting means that someone is demanding that something happen.

For example:
If you will smoke two packs of cigarettes a day, it's no wonder you have respiratory problems.

Won't can be used to politely express refusal when you use it with if. When you refuse to do something, it means that you don't want to do it. You are saying “no” to doing something.

For example:
If you won't pick me up later, I'll get a ride with my mother.

In speaking, you need to place more emphasis and stress on the word won't.
If you won't do it this month, the deal is off.
